In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the controlling mechanism of SOA formation cannot be inferred from laboratory data alone.
the mechanisms of SOA production are complex, and that the extent to which a specific mechanism is dominant can only be inferred from a combination of laboratory and ambient observations.

, while the partitioning of first-generation products is a necessary condition for SOA formation, it is not sufficient, and that the kinetics of particle-phase reactions can have a major impact on SOA yield and composition.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

SOA formation can proceed through either of the mechanisms of particle-phase reactions of first-generation products or gas-phase reactions of second-generation products, depending on the specific chemistry involved.
the formation of SOA from the oxidation of a parent hydrocarbon is controlled by a combination of partitioning and particle-phase reactions.

SOA yield is controlled by the kinetics of particle-phase reactions of semivolatiles, by the rate of parent oxidation, by the extent of oxidation of the parent hydrocarbons, and by the extent of pre-existing organic matter.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the controlling mechanisms of the formation of SOA from any given precursor are not unique, but depend on both the chemical and physical properties of the system.

, for a given system, there is a unique combination of gas- and aerosols-phase processes that can reproduce the observed SOA formation, so that a single set of observations cannot uniquely identify a mechanism.
the SOA yield and rate of formation are controlled by a combination of gas-phase and particle-phase reactions, which can be inferred from chamber data.
